title: Foreign-Owned Tertiary Hospitals, Outbound Medical Tourism, and Health Equity in Lagos State, Nigeria: A Qualitative Case Study
content: Healthcare systems in Low and middle-income countries (LMICs) often face inequitable access and inadequate infrastructure, contributing to outbound medical tourism (OMT). In Nigeria, foreign-owned tertiary hospitals (FOTHs) such as Evercare Hospital Lagos (Evercare) provide specialized services for wealthier patients. This research examined how FOTHs influence OMT and health equity and compared them with publicly owned tertiary hospitals (POTHs). It adopted a qualitative case study design, with eight participants purposively selected from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), Evercare, and Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH) for semi-structured interviews; evidence was analysed using process tracing and ATLAS.ti, with triangulation. Government support differed between FOTHs and POTHs, influencing OMT and health equity. While FOTHs modestly improved OMT by providing premium care domestically, their services remained accessible to affluent patients, leaving the remaining population dependent on overstretched POTHs. FOTHs showed potential to reduce OMT for high-income groups but did not significantly advance health equity in Nigeria. Addressing these issues entails institutional and regulatory reforms that require FOTHs to promote equity. The study was limited to Lagos and a small, targeted stakeholder sample, while OMT estimates relied on bank transactions and excluded parallel-market foreign-exchange transactions.
